essential_question: What routines keep people safe and ready to move well?
learning_objectives: Surface current control and understanding of self-space and general space under pressure, without scoring or comparison, and establish the unit question.
Use the movement cues for self-space and general space under pressure and explain or show why they work.
Adjust the task, equipment, or support for self-space and general space under pressure so it is safe and achievable, and describe the adjustment.
success_criteria: The learner takes part in the task about self-space and general space under pressure at a self-selected challenge level.
The learner uses or names the movement cues for self-space and general space under pressure.
The learner identifies one adjustment or next step. No score, time, count, or measurement is required.
materials: unit equipment listed in the guardian safety review
cues: Scan continuously; the space changes as others move.
Move into gaps rather than following the crowd.
Keep your head up even while controlling an object.
Anticipate where a gap will be, not where it is now.
common_error: Watching only the nearest person. Fix: set tasks requiring learners to call out a far gap before travelling to it.

lesson_flow.teacher_or_tutor_action: Confirm the space, surface, footwear, and equipment are safe, review the boundaries, and confirm the guardian safety review for this unit before any movement begins.
Lead a gradual warm-up that prepares the body for self-space and general space under pressure. The learner sets their own intensity and may rest at any point.

Demonstrate or describe self-space and general space under pressure and teach these cues explicitly, checking each before moving on:
  1. Scan continuously; the space changes as others move.
  2. Move into gaps rather than following the crowd.
  3. Keep your head up even while controlling an object.
  4. Anticipate where a gap will be, not where it is now.

The learner explores self-space and general space under pressure freely so the facilitator can see what they already control, with no correction and no scoring, at a self-selected challenge level and using the adapted alternative whenever it fits better. Watch for the common error: Watching only the nearest person. Fix: set tasks requiring learners to call out a far gap before travelling to it. Feedback names the cue, never the learner body or ability.

Cool down, then the learner names one thing about self-space and general space under pressure that already felt comfortable and one that felt new, and names one thing to adjust next time. No score, time, count, or measurement is recorded.

student_activity: The learner practises self-space and general space under pressure at a self-selected challenge level, using the adapted alternative whenever it fits better, and names the cue that helped.
formative_check: The learner names one cue that helped with self-space and general space under pressure and one adjustment for next time, by demonstrating, describing, drawing, or writing.
answer_or_scoring_guidance: Score cue use, control, decision-making, and explanation. Never score speed, distance, repetitions, body measurement, or comparison with another learner. Choosing the adapted path, a rest, or an opt-out is never scored as a deficit. Never infer effort, character, or ability from a movement outcome.

adaptive_tutor_routes.action: Return to the simplest version of self-space and general space under pressure — slower, closer, larger, or supported — then retry one fresh attempt.
Ask the learner to name the cue for self-space and general space under pressure and say why it works before continuing.
Confirm the specific cue the learner executed well for self-space and general space under pressure, offer one varied condition, and avoid unnecessary remediation.
Name the observable movement pattern neutrally, never as a comment on the learner body, effort, or character, contrast it with a demonstration, and schedule short varied practice.
Require controlled independent performance of self-space and general space under pressure plus an explanation on a later or different occasion before marking it mastered.

mastery_rule: Do not mark mastery from one attempt. Use observed control, cue use, decision-making, explanation, and applied performance; require accurate independent evidence and successful transfer on at least two separate occasions. Mastery is never determined by speed, distance, repetition count, body measurement, or comparison with another learner.
extension: Apply self-space and general space under pressure under one new condition of the learner choosing — different equipment, space, speed, or partner — and describe what changed.
accessibility_and_accommodations: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show or describe a model before practice.
Allow demonstrated, described, drawn, spoken, signed, or written evidence; the response mode is never the standard being assessed.
Offer reduced-repetition, extended-time, hidden-timer, rest-break, and low-stimulation options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for any media.
Preserve the movement target while adjusting equipment, distance, speed, force, duration, or support.
adapted_alternative: Every travel task has a seated, supported, or reduced-range version: a learner may move through space in a wheelchair or walker, travel a shorter path, use arms only, or trace the pathway with a pointer or on paper. Speed is never the target; control is. Where a task mentions a group or a partner, a learner may work with one adult instead, or plan and justify it on paper, and that counts fully.
safety_and_privacy: Use respectful, non-shaming language about bodies, ability, size, speed, and coordination.
Never require or record body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, or any body measurement.
Never require a fitness test, a timed trial, a repetition count, a distance score, or any ranking of one learner against another.
Never require a photograph, video, or any recording of the learner as proof of participation or performance.
Never require a public performance, an audience, or a demonstration in front of peers; sharing is always the learner choice.
Progress is compared only against the learner own earlier work, and only when the learner chooses to track it.
Allow rest, a break, an adapted path, or an opt-out at any point without treating it as failure.
Stop activity and seek a trusted adult or qualified professional for pain, dizziness, breathing difficulty, or injury; this course is not medical advice.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Open floor space clear of furniture and trip hazards; non-slip footwear or bare feet on a safe surface.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Indoor open space, gym, or a cleared room. An outdoor lawn may be substituted.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Running and stopping in shared space. Guardian confirms the area is clear, the floor is not slippery, and boundaries are marked before the session.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, cue card, or adult demonstration supporting self-space and general space under pressure.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable cue steps, alt text, a transcript, or a live adult demonstration. No recording of the learner is made.

parent_or_guardian_visibility: Share the lesson target, completion state, evidence type, the guardian safety confirmation for equipment and environment, and the next instructional step. Demonstrate or describe leading a moving receiver and teach these cues explicitly, checking each before moving on:
  1. Throw to where they will be, not where they are.
  2. Match the pass speed to their running speed.
  3. Aim slightly ahead and to their open side.
  4. Communicate before releasing.

Watch for the common error: Throwing behind a runner, which stops them. Fix: mark a target zone ahead of the receiver and aim into it. Feedback names the cue, never the learner body or ability.

Michigan PE Standard 4: Exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others
Michigan PE Standard 5: Recognizes the value of physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression and/or other benefits
essential_question: How do strategy, leadership, and inclusion make activity work for everyone?
learning_objectives: Surface current control and understanding of offensive and defensive space, without scoring or comparison, and establish the unit question.
Use the movement cues for offensive and defensive space and explain or show why they work.
Adjust the task, equipment, or support for offensive and defensive space so it is safe and achievable, and describe the adjustment.
success_criteria: The learner takes part in the task about offensive and defensive space at a self-selected challenge level.
The learner uses or names the movement cues for offensive and defensive space.
The learner identifies one adjustment or next step. No score, time, count, or measurement is required.
materials: unit equipment listed in the guardian safety review
cues: Attacking: spread out to create space.
Defending: close space and stay between the attacker and the goal.
Space is created by movement, not by standing still.
Watch where the space is opening, not only where the object is.
common_error: Everyone chasing the object. Fix: freeze play and ask each player to name the space they should be in.

lesson_flow.teacher_or_tutor_action: Confirm the space, surface, footwear, and equipment are safe, review the boundaries, and confirm the guardian safety review for this unit before any movement begins.
Lead a gradual warm-up that prepares the body for offensive and defensive space. The learner sets their own intensity and may rest at any point.

Demonstrate or describe offensive and defensive space and teach these cues explicitly, checking each before moving on:
  1. Attacking: spread out to create space.
  2. Defending: close space and stay between the attacker and the goal.
  3. Space is created by movement, not by standing still.
  4. Watch where the space is opening, not only where the object is.

The learner explores offensive and defensive space freely so the facilitator can see what they already control, with no correction and no scoring, at a self-selected challenge level and using the adapted alternative whenever it fits better. Watch for the common error: Everyone chasing the object. Fix: freeze play and ask each player to name the space they should be in. Feedback names the cue, never the learner body or ability.

Cool down, then the learner names one thing about offensive and defensive space that already felt comfortable and one that felt new, and names one thing to adjust next time. No score, time, count, or measurement is recorded.

student_activity: The learner practises offensive and defensive space at a self-selected challenge level, using the adapted alternative whenever it fits better, and names the cue that helped.
formative_check: The learner names one cue that helped with offensive and defensive space and one adjustment for next time, by demonstrating, describing, drawing, or writing.
answer_or_scoring_guidance: Score cue use, control, decision-making, and explanation. Never score speed, distance, repetitions, body measurement, or comparison with another learner. Choosing the adapted path, a rest, or an opt-out is never scored as a deficit. Never infer effort, character, or ability from a movement outcome.

adaptive_tutor_routes.action: Return to the simplest version of offensive and defensive space — slower, closer, larger, or supported — then retry one fresh attempt.
Ask the learner to name the cue for offensive and defensive space and say why it works before continuing.
Confirm the specific cue the learner executed well for offensive and defensive space, offer one varied condition, and avoid unnecessary remediation.
Name the observable movement pattern neutrally, never as a comment on the learner body, effort, or character, contrast it with a demonstration, and schedule short varied practice.
Require controlled independent performance of offensive and defensive space plus an explanation on a later or different occasion before marking it mastered.

mastery_rule: Do not mark mastery from one attempt. Use observed control, cue use, decision-making, explanation, and applied performance; require accurate independent evidence and successful transfer on at least two separate occasions. Mastery is never determined by speed, distance, repetition count, body measurement, or comparison with another learner.
extension: Apply offensive and defensive space under one new condition of the learner choosing — different equipment, space, speed, or partner — and describe what changed.
accessibility_and_accommodations: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show or describe a model before practice.
Allow demonstrated, described, drawn, spoken, signed, or written evidence; the response mode is never the standard being assessed.
Offer reduced-repetition, extended-time, hidden-timer, rest-break, and low-stimulation options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for any media.
Preserve the movement target while adjusting equipment, distance, speed, force, duration, or support.
adapted_alternative: Games are adapted so every learner has a real role: adjustable boundaries, extra passes, a designated safe zone, a slower or larger object, a seated or stationary position, and role options including player, coach, official, or strategist. Any rule may be changed to include a learner rather than excluding them. Where a task asks the learner to lead or officiate, they may lead one adult, officiate a scripted scenario, or write and justify the plan instead; leading is never done in front of an audience.
safety_and_privacy: Use respectful, non-shaming language about bodies, ability, size, speed, and coordination.
Never require or record body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, or any body measurement.
Never require a fitness test, a timed trial, a repetition count, a distance score, or any ranking of one learner against another.
Never require a photograph, video, or any recording of the learner as proof of participation or performance.
Never require a public performance, an audience, or a demonstration in front of peers; sharing is always the learner choice.
Progress is compared only against the learner own earlier work, and only when the learner chooses to track it.
Allow rest, a break, an adapted path, or an opt-out at any point without treating it as failure.
Stop activity and seek a trusted adult or qualified professional for pain, dizziness, breathing difficulty, or injury; this course is not medical advice.

guardian_safety_review.equipment: Cones or markers, soft balls, and any protective gear the chosen activity needs.
guardian_safety_review.environment: Supervised outdoor area or indoor open space, away from roads, water, and parking areas.
guardian_safety_review.movement_hazards: Small-sided play involves changing direction near others, with collision risk. Guardian sets boundaries, group size, and contact rules, and checks the surface and weather before play.
guardian_safety_review.food_or_allergy_note: Provide water for outdoor sessions; check any insect-sting or seasonal-allergy plan already in place.
